clue.text: Like a couple of times with the spy group Little Edward? Tied in this way!

parts.note: as means like, in comparisons
like is meant a second time, now as so, which also means in the same way
the CIA is the US Central Intelligence Agency
Ted is a pet form of Edward

explanation.surface: A spy ring's young Edward, bound up with it more than once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like a couple of times' asks for two words meaning like, AS and SO, followed by CIA and TED.
explanation.definitionFit: Being associated with something means being linked or connected to it, tied in.

clue.text: Possibly the location of a side street, with a serving of drinks on the seasoner.

definitions.text: Possibly the location of a side street

parts.note: a round is one set of drinks bought for a group
taken as written
a corner is one who corns meat, curing it with salt as in corned beef

explanation.surface: A bar on a side street that serves drinks with salt on the side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corn' means to preserve with salt, so a corner is cryptically something that seasons.
explanation.definitionFit: A side street typically branches off a main road, so it is often found just round the bend from it.

clue.text: Made a face, because Bossy gets to go downhill around it.

indicators.note: the sled goes around Bossy, so its letters enclose the others

parts.note: to sled is to slide downhill on a sledge
Bossy is a traditional American pet name for a cow

explanation.surface: Someone grimacing at a cow tobogganing down a slope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' signals a container, with the downhill ride enclosing the cow. Bossy is the stock name for a cow in American farm talk, as Daisy is in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: To scowl is to frown angrily, which is pulling an expression of displeasure.

clue.text: Johnny might be kept in the register.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Johnny ..., the country singer

definitions.text: might be kept in the register

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests someone named in a list; the register is a shop till.
explanation.definitionFit: The country singer's surname is also the word for coins and notes, which a cash register holds.

clue.text: Attack like Ste. Marie?

parts.note: as means like, in the way of
Sault Ste. Marie is a city on the US-Canada border, so the word before Ste. Marie is Sault

explanation.surface: An assault modelled on a saint, apparently.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the trick: Ste. Marie is not a saint but the end of the place name Sault Ste. Marie, which straddles Michigan and Ontario.
explanation.definitionFit: An assault is a violent physical attack.

clue.text: The last ice cream shows what is stretchable.

indicators.note: the word shows itself, sitting visible within the phrase

parts.note: the letters run across thE LAST ICe

explanation.surface: The final scoop of ice cream reveals something that can stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: Elastic material returns to shape after being pulled, so it is stretchable.

clue.text: Makes out, but 13 at first.

parts.note: 13 across begins with just, so this means makes out, but only just, as one scrapes by

explanation.walkthrough: The first word of 13 across is JUST, so the clue reads 'makes out, but just': to eke out a living is to manage it barely.
explanation.definitionFit: To eke out is to scrape by on scant means, getting along only narrowly.

clue.text: The little type is taking a snooze. (Takes a child too, possibly.)

parts.note: a kid is a child, a little person
naps means takes a short sleep

explanation.surface: A small child dozing off, and possibly another being carried away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Too' tells you the second half is another reading of the same word: one who kidnaps takes away a child.
explanation.definitionFit: To kidnap is to abduct someone, originally and literally a child, as the word itself says.

clue.text: Showing what the ego is all about? (You need no more info, if so.)

definitions.text: Showing what the ego is all about?
definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: explaining the self, the ego

definitions.text: You need no more info, if so
definitions.meaning: second meaning: clear on its own, needing no further explanation

explanation.walkthrough: The first reading splits the word into self and explanatory; the second is the ordinary sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Something self-explanatory is obvious enough that it requires no further clarification.

clue.text: The ocean has a sort of satin finish, as one insists.

indicators.note: the ocean has the rest after it, so the pieces are joined in this order

parts.note: the main is an old poetic word for the open sea

indicators.note: a sort of satin is a version of the word with its letters shuffled

explanation.surface: The sea's surface has a satiny sheen, someone insists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has' puts MAIN first; 'sort of' turns SATIN into TAINS, which is the finish of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To maintain a claim is to assert it firmly, as someone who insists does.

clue.text: They might be found blowing in the winds.

definitions.text: They might be found blowing in the winds

parts.words: They might be found blowing in the winds
parts.note: the winds are an orchestra's woodwind section, where these reed players blow, not gusts of weather

explanation.surface: Things carried along by blowing gales.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The winds' sounds like the weather, but in an orchestra the winds are the woodwind players.
explanation.definitionFit: Players of the oboe sit in the woodwind section and produce sound by blowing through a double reed.

clue.text: Like the three blind mice, when Mrs. Farmer caught up with them.

definitions.text: Like the three blind mice, when Mrs. Farmer caught up with them

parts.words: Like the three blind mice, when Mrs. Farmer caught up with them
parts.note: in the nursery rhyme the farmer's wife cuts off their tails with a carving knife, leaving them without tails

explanation.surface: The nursery-rhyme mice after the farmer's wife has dealt with them.
explanation.walkthrough: The rhyme has the farmer's wife cut off the mice's tails, so the answer is the zoological word for having no tail.
explanation.definitionFit: Acaudal is a biological term meaning tailless, which is how the mice ended up after the carving knife.

clue.text: This represents nothing.

parts.note: a word for zero, an empty value or something of no legal force

explanation.walkthrough: A plain description of a word meaning zero or void, as in 'null and void' or a null set in mathematics.
explanation.definitionFit: Null means amounting to nothing: a null set is empty and a null contract has no force.

clue.text: Very fair in the trial, with extra care.

parts.note: just means fair and right, as a just ruling is
a case is a lawsuit tried in court

explanation.surface: A judge being scrupulously fair during a court hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: The courtroom surface hides a charade: JUST, then IN as written, then CASE.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something just in case means taking a precaution beyond what is strictly needed.

clue.text: The press and radio turn into what the arbitrator should excel in.

definitions.text: what the arbitrator should excel in

parts.note: newspapers and broadcasting together are the media

indicators.note: turn means the letters of into are turned about into a new order

explanation.surface: Newspapers and broadcasters becoming what a referee ought to be good at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into' looks like a link word joining the halves of the surface, but 'turn' makes it the anagram fodder, giving TION.
explanation.definitionFit: Mediation is negotiating a settlement between parties, the core skill of a good arbitrator.

clue.text: It comes back to pass on a little way–which is neat to the nth!

indicators.note: something coming back returns the way it came, so the word it is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written before being turned round
to pass on is a euphemism for to die
ST is the abbreviation for street, a little way or road

explanation.surface: Something going back to deliver a message a short distance, done with extreme tidiness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'comes back' turns IT into TI. 'To the nth' means to the utmost degree, so the definition asks for a superlative.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of tidy describes the most orderly possible, neat to the highest degree.

clue.text: Ain't saying a thing! (Seafood to have a little meal!)

parts.note: a clam is an edible shellfish
to sup is to eat a light supper

explanation.surface: A tight-lipped diner refusing to talk over a light seafood supper.
explanation.definitionFit: To clam up is an idiom for going silent and refusing to say anything, as a closed clam shell does.

clue.text: A tender skin eventually shows up the writer.

indicators.note: the name shows up, plainly visible, inside the run of clue words

parts.note: the letters run across tendER SKIN Eventually

explanation.surface: A sore patch of skin finally revealing who did the writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shows up' points to the name lying across 'tender skin eventually'. John Erskine was an American novelist and critic, author of The Private Life of Helen of Troy.
explanation.definitionFit: John Erskine was a twentieth-century American author, so his surname names a writer.

clue.text: Came forth with a point associated with it. (Sort of dies round every bit!)

parts.note: S is south, a point of the compass
allied means associated or joined

explanation.surface: Emerging with a sharp tip, and a die rolled round every piece.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed second part is an alternative wordplay: an anagram ('Sort of') of DIES around ALL ('every bit').
explanation.definitionFit: To sally forth is to set out or emerge suddenly, as troops did from a besieged town.

clue.text: Appearing before anything else, noble, but with an outburst of ire.

parts.note: an earl is a nobleman

indicators.note: an outburst scatters the letters of ire into a new order

explanation.surface: A nobleman coming first but losing his temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outburst of' is the anagram signal, the angry burst scattering the letters of 'ire' into IER.
explanation.definitionFit: Earlier means coming at a previous time, ahead of what follows.

clue.text: The wrong name is wrong with a forgetful condition.

indicators.note: something wrong is out of order, so these letters must be rearranged
the repeat stresses that the letters are muddled, putting the final a into the mix too

explanation.surface: Getting someone's name wrong because of a memory problem.
explanation.walkthrough: Both uses of 'wrong' call for a rearrangement: muddle the letters of NAME, IS and A together.
explanation.definitionFit: Amnesia is a medical condition involving loss of memory, so a forgetful state.

clue.text: They reputedly have a louder voice than your speech implies. (The first part of the play has no upbringing, to a point.)

definitions.text: They reputedly have a louder voice than your speech implies

parts.words: The first part of the play
parts.note: Act I is the opening act of a play

indicators.note: in a down clue bringing up means reading the word no from the bottom up

parts.note: S is south, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: Acts speaking louder than words, and a play's first act lacking breeding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upbringing' brings NO up the column as ON. The definition plays on the saying 'actions speak louder than words'.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb holds that deeds say more about someone than what they say.

clue.text: One of a Far East warrior group, like our uncle at the old city, first-class!

definitions.text: One of a Far East warrior group

parts.note: Uncle Sam personifies the United States, the setter's home
Ur is the ancient Mesopotamian city
A1 means first-rate, written here as AI

explanation.surface: A Japanese warrior compared to an American uncle in an ancient city.
explanation.walkthrough: The Nation is an American magazine, so 'our uncle' is Uncle Sam.
explanation.definitionFit: Samurai were members of the hereditary warrior class of feudal Japan.

clue.text: Scrub it!

parts.note: an order to wipe something out completely, scrubbing it away until no trace is left

explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrub' looks like cleaning, but here it means cancel or erase entirely.
explanation.definitionFit: To obliterate is to destroy or erase utterly, the way scrubbing removes a mark.

clue.text: A writing due to Mame, otherwise?

indicators.note: otherwise means arranged differently, so the letters of Mame are reordered

explanation.surface: A text written by Auntie Mame, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'otherwise' asks for MAME arranged differently. Mame is the heroine of the novel and musical Auntie Mame; the answer is a novel by Jane Austen.
explanation.definitionFit: Emma is Jane Austen's 1815 novel, so it is a piece of writing.

clue.text: The place for pigs has a point, but you wouldn't want it in your eye!

definitions.text: you wouldn't want it in your eye

parts.note: a sty is a pigpen
E is east, a point of the compass

explanation.surface: A pigpen with a sharp point, best kept away from your eye.
explanation.definitionFit: A stye is a painful inflamed swelling on the eyelid.

clue.text: Place where there's a point to the tune, with a sash on…

parts.note: N is north, a point of the compass
an air is a tune
an obi is the broad sash worn with a kimono

explanation.surface: A spot where a melody comes to a head, with someone wearing a sash.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links this clue to the next, which is also a place.
explanation.definitionFit: Nairobi is the capital city of Kenya, a place in East Africa.

clue.text: …and a place much farther north where the tune is mixed onto the surroundings.

indicators.note: onto acts as the surroundings, so its letters wrap round the others

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a mixed tune has its letters stirred into a new order

parts.note: an air is a tune

explanation.surface: Somewhere up north where a tune gets mixed in with its setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is mixed' scrambles the tune into ARI, and 'the surroundings' makes 'onto' wrap round it. It follows on from the Nairobi clue: Ontario lies far north of Kenya.
explanation.definitionFit: Ontario is a Canadian province, a place lying well north of Nairobi in the previous clue.

clue.text: Describing an arching bridge, which is not very polite.

definitions.meaning: first meaning: Emerson's Concord Hymn opens 'By the ... bridge that arched the flood', so the adjective is the one used of that bridge

explanation.walkthrough: The first half quotes Emerson's Concord Hymn on the battle at Concord: 'By the rude bridge that arched the flood'. There rude means roughly made.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means both crudely built, as of a simple bridge, and lacking good manners.

clue.text: Once said to be the head of 13 with 1 down.

definitions.text: Once said to be the head of 13 with 1 down

parts.words: Once said to be the head of 13 with 1 down
parts.note: the Depression-era promise that this was 'just around the corner': it heads a sentence built from the answers to 13 and 1 down

explanation.walkthrough: Herbert Hoover's administration kept assuring Americans during the Depression that prosperity was just around the corner; 13 gives JUST IN CASE's first word and 1 down AROUND THE CORNER.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the subject of the famous optimistic slogan about economic recovery being imminent.
